opus-5.5.text:
I think Moravec's paradox is one of the most useful lenses for thinking about where AI actually is today. The original observation, from Hans Moravec and others back in the eighties, was that the things we consider hard — chess, calculus, formal logic — turned out to be relatively easy for computers, while the things a one-year-old does effortlessly — recognizing a face, grabbing a cup, walking across a messy room — turned out to be incredibly hard.

The way I understand it, "easy" and "difficult" for humans are really a reflection of evolutionary history, not intrinsic complexity. Perception, motor control, spatial understanding — these abilities were refined over hundreds of millions of years. They're so deeply optimized in us that they feel effortless, and because they're unconscious, we don't even recognize them as intelligence. Abstract reasoning, language, mathematics are very recent in evolutionary terms. They feel hard to us precisely because our brains aren't that well-tuned for them yet. So what humans perceive as difficult is often just what's new.

For AI, I'd frame it in terms of data and representation. Tasks become easy for AI when the problem is already expressed in a compact, symbolic, human-curated form. Language is a great example. Text is a highly compressed abstraction of the world that humans already did the hard work of producing. When large language models learn from trillions of tokens, they're inheriting the output of human cognition. That's partly why LLMs advanced so fast — and why it looks like the paradox is being confirmed again: writing essays, passing exams, even coding came before reliably folding laundry.

The difficult tasks are the ones where you have to deal with the raw, continuous, high-dimensional physical world directly — pixels, video, touch, physics, causality, three-dimensional space. There's no pre-digested abstraction. You need to build your own representations from sensory input, and you need to ground them in action and consequence. That's exactly where today's systems are still weak. A model can describe how to pour water into a glass, but genuinely understanding the geometry, the dynamics, what happens if you tilt it a bit more — that kind of grounded, embodied understanding is still very far from solved.

That's why I personally care a lot about visual intelligence and spatial intelligence. I don't think language alone will get us to a full understanding of the world. Language is like the tip of the iceberg; underneath is a huge mass of perceptual and physical knowledge that humans never bother to write down because it's too obvious to us. If we want AI systems that can truly operate in the real world — robots, agents, things that understand space and time — we have to tackle the "easy" half of Moravec's paradox, which is actually the hard half. In a way, the paradox is telling us where the real frontier is.

r001.rationale: It contrasts skills effortless for humans, such as face recognition and walking, but hard for computers, with abstract tasks like chess and calculus that are hard for humans but relatively easy for computers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Moravec's paradox is one of the most important lenses for understanding where we actually are in AI right now. The basic observation is that things humans find hard, like playing chess or Go, doing symbolic math, writing code, turned out to be relatively easy for machines. And the things we find effortless, like a toddler picking up a cup, recognizing that a cat is still a cat when it's half hidden behind a sofa, walking across a cluttered room, those have been incredibly hard.

The way I understand it is through evolutionary time. Perception and motor control have been optimized by hundreds of millions of years of evolution. These are deep, ancient capabilities, and because they're so old and so refined, they feel automatic to us. We have no introspective access to how hard they actually are. Abstract reasoning, language, mathematics, these are recent inventions, maybe a few hundred thousand years at most, and they run on top of that older machinery. They feel hard because we are consciously doing them, step by step. So our intuition about what is "difficult" is basically backwards. It's measuring conscious effort, not computational complexity.

For me, working in vision, this is very personal, because vision is exactly the thing the paradox warns you about. People look at ImageNet classification or image generation and think, okay, vision is solved. But the real task of vision is not labeling an image. It's building a model of the world, understanding space, objects, physics, permanence, causality, from sensory input that is noisy and partial. That's the part evolution spent all its effort on, and I don't think we're close to it. Language models have made enormous progress partly because language is already a compressed, symbolic representation created by humans. The hard work of grounding was done by us before the text was ever written. A vision system doesn't get that gift. It has to do the grounding itself.

So the practical lesson I take is that we should be suspicious whenever a benchmark feels like it rewards the "human-hard" kind of intelligence. The frontier is not getting better at things we already find hard. The frontier is the stuff we never had to think about. And that's where I think the next decade of work, especially in visual and embodied intelligence, really is.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks humans find hard, such as chess, are relatively easy for machines, while effortless human skills like perception and movement have been incredibly hard for machines.

astra-6.text:
I think Moravec’s paradox tells us that what feels easy to humans isn’t necessarily easy for AI. We tend to associate intelligence with things like solving mathematical problems or playing chess. But for a computer, those tasks can be easier than recognizing an object in an unfamiliar environment or controlling a robot hand to pick it up.

One way to understand that is through evolution. Perception and motor control have been refined over an enormous amount of time. We do them almost unconsciously, so we underestimate how much computation they require. Abstract reasoning is relatively recent, and because it takes conscious effort, we think of it as the harder problem.

So when we ask whether a task is easy or difficult for AI, human effort is a misleading yardstick. We need to look at what information the system has, what it has learned, and how much uncertainty it needs to handle. A task that’s straightforward in a carefully defined setting can become very difficult in the open world.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks that feel easy to humans, such as object recognition and motor control, can be harder for AI than abstract tasks like math or chess, capturing the reversal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Moravec’s paradox tells us that our intuition about difficulty is very human-centered. We tend to think that abstract reasoning, playing chess, or solving mathematical problems is hard, while recognizing an object or picking up a cup is easy. But for AI, that ordering can be reversed.

The things we do effortlessly are supported by an enormous amount of biological evolution and experience. We don’t consciously notice all the computation involved in perception and movement. Picking up a cup means understanding its shape, estimating where it is, controlling your fingers, and adapting to feedback. What feels like one simple action actually contains many difficult problems.

So I would distinguish between a task being easy to perform and being easy to describe. Chess has explicit rules and a clear objective. Many everyday tasks are much harder to specify, even though a child can do them. From that perspective, the paradox is a reminder that human effort is not a reliable measure of computational difficulty. We need to look at the structure of the task, the available data, and how the system learns.

r001.rationale: It says humans see abstract reasoning as hard and perception or movement as easy, while “for AI, that ordering can be reversed.”
